opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think this is one of the most interesting questions right now. The way I frame it is that we've been in a regime where progress was largely driven by scaling up models on human-generated data: the internet, books, code. That's been incredibly productive, but it's fundamentally a finite resource, and in a sense it also puts a ceiling on things, because you're learning to imitate the distribution of what humans have already produced.

So the question becomes: how do you turn compute into new knowledge, or new data, without needing more from the real world? And I think the answer that history keeps pointing us towards is environments and self-play. If you look at AlphaGo and then AlphaZero, the key insight was that once you have a simulator, a set of rules, the agent can generate its own experience, and the quality of that experience goes up as the agent gets better. You get this kind of autocurriculum where the opponent, or the environment, co-evolves with the learner. That's a way of converting compute directly into capability, and it doesn't saturate the way a fixed dataset does.

A lot of my work, especially in multi-agent learning and in open-endedness, is really about trying to generalize that recipe beyond board games. How do you build environments that are rich enough, and procedurally generated enough, that agents trained in them actually acquire general skills? How do you get unsupervised environment design, where one process is proposing tasks at the frontier of what the learner can do? And then, with JAX and running everything on the accelerator, things like end-to-end GPU-based environments, you can suddenly run thousands of times more experience per second, which changes the kinds of research questions you can even ask.

Then there's the LLM side of this, which is where things have gotten really exciting. Language models give you a prior over what's interesting and meaningful to humans, so they can act as task generators, as judges, as the "world" in some sense. And reasoning with verifiable rewards, math, code, things where you can check the answer, is essentially the same idea: you have a verifier, so you can generate unlimited training signal by sampling and checking. The bottleneck shifts from data to verification and to the design of the search process.

Now, I want to be careful not to overclaim. Compute-only scaling isn't magic. You need some grounding, some signal that ties back to what we actually care about. If your simulator is wrong, or your verifier can be gamed, you'll happily scale your way into reward hacking. And for domains like biology or the physical world, eventually you have to close the loop with reality, run the experiment. So I think the real frontier is figuring out how to use compute to make every bit of real-world interaction maximally informative: better simulators, better self-generated curricula, and then very targeted contact with the real world where it matters.

But broadly, yes, I'm optimistic. I think the next phase of progress is going to look less like "collect a bigger dataset" and more like "design the right game and let the agents play it."

r001.rationale: The response proposes training agents in simulators and richer environments, but it does not clearly propose discovering algorithms in fast, imperfect simulations that generalize to real-world tasks.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So I think this is actually one of the most important questions in the field right now, and my answer is that compute-only scaling, where you keep the data fixed and just pour more flops into the system, is going to look very different depending on what kind of problem you're working on.

Let me separate two regimes. In the first regime, you're trying to learn about the world. Language, images, physics, biology. Here the data is the thing, right? The information about the world has to come from somewhere, and if you've already scraped the internet, more compute on the same data gives you diminishing returns fairly quickly. You can squeeze a bit more out with better algorithms, more epochs, smarter curricula, but fundamentally you're bounded by the entropy of what you've collected. I don't think anyone serious disputes that.

But there's a second regime, which is the one I've spent most of my career in, and that's settings where you have a simulator or an environment that can generate experience for you. Games, multi-agent systems, code, mathematics, anything with a verifier. And in that regime, the picture flips completely. Compute is data. Every additional unit of compute you spend on self-play, on search, on exploring the environment, literally produces new training signal that didn't exist before. AlphaZero is the canonical example: zero human games, and it just keeps getting better the longer you let it run. There's no ceiling imposed by a dataset because the dataset is manufactured on the fly.

Now the interesting thing, and this is where I'd push back a bit on how people frame it, is that these two regimes are converging. Reasoning models, RL on verifiable rewards, test-time compute, all of that is essentially taking the second paradigm and importing it into the first. You've got a base model that absorbed the world knowledge from the finite data, and then you spend compute to generate rollouts, score them, and train on the ones that were good. That's self-play in disguise. The human data gives you the prior, and compute gives you the posterior, if you like.

So where does that leave us when real-world data gets scarce? My honest view is that the binding constraint shifts from "how much data do you have" to "how good is your environment and your reward signal." If you can build a faithful simulator or a reliable verifier for a domain, then scaling compute in that domain is close to unbounded. If you can't, if the only ground truth is messy human preference or real-world outcomes that take months to observe, then compute alone won't save you, and you'll see the same plateau that people worry about.

And this is why I get a bit excited rather than worried. The research question becomes: how do we design environments and curricula so that the agent generates its own useful data? That's open-endedness, that's unsupervised environment design, which is work I've been doing with Michael Dennis and others. Instead of hand-picking tasks, you let the system search over the space of tasks itself, always finding the ones at the frontier of what it can currently do. Compute drives the curriculum, the curriculum produces data, and the data drives capability. It's a loop, and the thing you're scaling is the loop, not just a static dataset.

The caveat I'd add is about the sim-to-real gap. Everything I've described works beautifully inside the box. The moment you need the resulting capabilities to transfer to the actual world, you reintroduce the data problem through the back door, because you need some real-world signal to tell you whether your simulator was faithful. So I'd say compute-only scaling buys you an enormous amount in the domains where you can close that gap, which is more domains than people think, and it buys you a lot less in the domains where you can't. The craft is in knowing which one you're in.

r001.rationale: The response discusses generating experience in simulators and the sim-to-real gap, but it does not propose discovering algorithms in fast, imperfect simulations that generalize to real-world tasks.

astra-6.text:
I think the exciting possibility is that we can use computation to generate the experience we learn from, rather than relying entirely on collecting more data from the world. Reinforcement learning gives us a way of doing that: an agent tries things, gets feedback, and improves. In self-play, the agents themselves can create increasingly challenging problems for one another.

But there’s an important caveat: you need an environment and a feedback signal that actually reward the behaviour you care about. More compute doesn’t automatically give you better learning. An agent can become extremely good at exploiting a simulator without learning something useful outside it.

So I see compute-only scaling as a very promising direction, but also as an algorithmic challenge. How do we turn additional computation into useful exploration, better curricula, and experience that transfers? That’s where I think a lot of the interesting research lies.

r001.rationale: The response discusses reinforcement learning, self-play, and the risk of exploiting a simulator, but it does not propose discovering algorithms in fast, imperfect simulations that generalize to real-world tasks.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the exciting possibility is that more compute can buy us better learning, rather than simply letting us process more data. If progress depends on ever larger datasets, eventually we run into a constraint. So the question becomes: with the experience we already have, can we use additional computation to extract more from it?

Reinforcement learning offers one route, particularly where you can generate experience through interaction or self-play. You can spend compute exploring, testing strategies, and producing a curriculum that gets harder as the agent improves. Search is another example: you spend more computation thinking through a decision before acting.

But there’s an important qualification: generating more experience is only useful if it teaches you something relevant. An agent can get very good at a simulator and still fail in the real world. So I see compute-only scaling as a very promising direction, but the challenge is finding learning processes where additional computation reliably produces new capability, and where that capability transfers to the problems we care about.

r001.rationale: The response discusses interaction, self-play, and simulator experience, but does not propose discovering algorithms in fast, imperfect simulations that generalize to real-world tasks. It instead cautions that simulator capability may fail to transfer.
